```{r missing-deps, echo=FALSE, eval=!runs, results='asis'}

    "run.** Install them with `install.packages(c(\"gstat\", \"ggplot2\"))`",

```

*This article needs two optional packages: **gstat**, which fits the variogram
behind the autocorrelation range, and **ggplot2** for the figures. When either
is missing the code is shown but not run, and a note at the top says so.*

## The question

Before point observations can be aggregated into regions, something has to
decide how many regions. Twenty cells over a county smooth away most of the
variation you came to measure. Two thousand give you cells holding one
observation each, where the standard errors are undefined and every cell mean is
one number pretending to be an average.

Administrative boundaries settle this by fiat: you get the census tracts that
exist. Drawing the regions yourself removes the fiat and leaves the decision
with you, and the number propagates into the variance of the cell means, the
design effect, and the size of the blocks a spatial cross-validation holds out.

Three functions answer the question, in increasing order of how much they tell
you. `determine_optimal_levels()` reads an elbow off the coordinates alone and
runs on the hard dependencies; it is the quick answer and the one
`build_tessellation()` accepts directly. `resolution_profile()` scores every
cell count on a ladder in four columns at once, three count criteria and one
diagnostic, and needs gstat for two of them. `select_resolution()` reads one
criterion off that profile, and `summary()` on the profile reads the count
criteria side by side. If the cells will feed
a model, the profile is the one to use. If you need a count now and the data
are all you have, the elbow is defensible when the points cluster, and this
article says where it falls short. On points spread evenly there is no elbow
to read, and both functions say so: the profile leaves its `elbow` column
empty, and `determine_optimal_levels()` warns that the count it still returns
was chosen by the ends of its ladder, not by the data.

The argument that says "how many" is spelled differently by the function it
belongs to: `max_levels` bounds the elbow's ladder, `n_levels` sets the
profile's, `approx_n_cells` and `target_cells` are what the grid builders
take, and `n` is what `get_voronoi_seeds()` takes. Each of the last three
accepts the object the first two return.

## A fixture with known structure

A simulated exponential field, so the structure is known before anything is
fitted. The covariance parameter `a = 100` gives an effective range of 300 units
across a 1000-unit square, and `sd = 1` adds a nugget large enough to matter
later.

```{r fixture}
library(sf)
library(spatialkit)

set.seed(42)
n  <- 500
xy <- data.frame(x = 5e5 + runif(n, 0, 1000), y = 5e6 + runif(n, 0, 1000))
D  <- as.matrix(dist(xy))
xy$z <- as.numeric(t(chol(exp(-D / 100) + diag(1e-8, n))) %*% rnorm(n)) +
        rnorm(n, sd = 1)
pts  <- st_as_sf(xy, coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632)
```

## The short answer

`determine_optimal_levels()` returns a few candidate cell counts, best first.

```{r doi}
lv <- determine_optimal_levels(pts, max_levels = 40)
lv
```

This fixture's points are uniform, so their within-cluster sum of squares falls
like `c / k` all the way down and bends nowhere of its own. The call warns that
it found no elbow and that `max_levels` chose `lv`: a larger `max_levels` would
give a larger answer. Read an elbow only off points that cluster; here the
profile below is the better guide.

`lv[1]` is what `get_voronoi_seeds()` takes as `n`, and what
`build_tessellation()` takes as `approx_n_cells` for its `"hex"` and `"square"`
methods. Voronoi has no cell count to set: it grows one cell per point you hand
it, which is why the count is set when you place the seeds rather than when you
tessellate them. The last section shows the two calls in order.

Two things to know about this function before you rely on it. Its
`criterion = "morans_i"` and `criterion = "combined"` settings rank the counts
around the elbow by Moran's z of the cell means, which is a diagnostic and not
a count rule; the call returns the ranking with a warning of class
`spatialkit_diagnostic_ranking` that says so. They need a `response_var`;
without one the call warns and falls back to `"geometric"`. And its ladder
runs from 1 to `max_levels` with no lower bound from the spatial correlation
of the data, so it can prefer cells wider than the field's own correlation
range. The profile below reports that bound, and `select_resolution()` reads
`reliability` from it up, which is why the two can disagree.

## The profile

`resolution_profile()` fits every level on a ladder and reports what each one
costs, so you can see the shape of the trade-off before picking a point on it.
Levels are spaced logarithmically, because cell diameter falls as
\(L^{-1/2}\).

```{r profile}
prof <- resolution_profile(pts, response_var = "z", n_levels = 16)
prof
```

One row per level. `cell_n_median` and `cell_diam_median` are usually the first
two columns worth reading: how many points a typical cell holds, and how big it
is in CRS units. `cell_diam_median` is twice the median root-mean-square
distance of a cell's points from its centre, about 0.8 of the side of a square
cell of the same area, so compare it against something you already know about
your own data, such as the spacing of a sampling grid or the size of a field,
with that factor in mind.

### Three criteria and a diagnostic

```{r criteria-table, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
cat(
"| criterion | measures | needs | direction |\n",
"|---|---|---|---|\n",
"| `elbow` | how far the log of the within-cluster sum of squares sags below a power law (the straight log-log line from one cell to the last level); `NA` at every level when the points have no cluster structure | coordinates only | larger |\n",
"| `cp` | Mallows' \\(C_p\\) of the piecewise-constant approximation of the response by cell means | a response, and a variogram for the nugget | smaller |\n",
"| `moran_z` | Moran's z of the cell means (of their regression residuals when predictors are given): whether neighbouring cells resemble each other | a response | a diagnostic, not a count rule |\n",
"| `reliability` | the share of the spread in the cell means that is signal, not sampling noise | a variogram | larger |\n",
sep = "")
```

`elbow` sees the coordinates and knows nothing about what you measured. `cp` and
`reliability` split the practical question in half: how well the cells represent
the field, and whether the cell values can be told apart from noise. What `cp`
estimates is the error of re-measuring the sampled sites, each predicted by the
mean of its cell, with the variogram's nugget as the noise of one measurement.
For a new location the penalty would also need the spread of the field inside a
cell, which the nugget leaves out. `moran_z`
is a diagnostic of the cell means and not a count rule. It grows as the cells
get finer than the range, because neighbouring cells then resemble each other,
and it is near zero at the coarsest counts it is computed at whatever the data.
It does not say how well the cells represent the response, so
`select_resolution()` refuses it unless asked with `diagnostic = TRUE`, and
`summary()` leaves it out unless it is named.

```{r plot-profile, fig.height=8, fig.alt="Three stacked panels against the number of cells on a shared axis, from 2 to 55; there is no elbow panel because these uniform points have no elbow. Mallows' Cp falls across the ladder and is lowest at the last level, 55 cells. Reliability rises to a peak near 5 cells and declines after it. The absolute Moran's z of the cell means is drawn from 12 cells on, stays near 1 or below up to 28 cells and climbs past 3 at 55. A red dot and dotted line mark the level selected for Cp, at 55 cells, and for reliability, at 17 cells, with a shaded band over the levels within tolerance of each; the Moran panel has no selected level."}
plot(prof)
```

Two behaviours are worth knowing before reading the numbers.

```{r cp-context, echo=FALSE}
vg  <- attr(prof, "variogram")
nug <- round(vg$nugget, 2); psl <- round(vg$psill, 2)
cp_sel <- select_resolution(prof, criterion = "cp")
```

**`cp` needs a nugget to have an interior optimum.** On a smooth field the
piecewise-constant approximation keeps improving as cells shrink, the penalty is
too small to stop it, and the minimum lands wherever `min_cell_n` stops the
ladder. The support ceiling is then doing the choosing, and
`select_resolution()` flags it.

```{r cp-text, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
cat(sprintf("This fixture has a fitted nugget of %s against a partial sill of %s,", nug, psl),
    if (isTRUE(cp_sel$at_ceiling))
      "and `cp` still falls to the last level of the ladder here: its minimum is the support ceiling, as `summary()` says below.\n"
    else
      "which is why `cp` turns around inside the ladder here.\n")
```

**`reliability` is highest at a coarse count**, because bigger cells hold more
points and average away more noise. Its maximum usually lies below the range
floor, where cells are wider than the range. `select_resolution()` therefore
reads it from the floor up, and what it returns is then the floor: a bound on
the analysis, with the range choosing and not the curve. The next section is
about spotting that.

## Choosing, and the flat region

`select_resolution()` picks the level a criterion prefers and reports the band
around it.

```{r select}
sel <- select_resolution(prof, criterion = "reliability")
sel
```

`sel$best` is the optimum and `sel$flat` is every level within `tol` of it.
Quote the band when you write the analysis up. `tol` is relative to the
optimum's value for `cp` and `reliability`, and relative to the criterion's
range for `elbow` and `moran_z`, whose optima can be zero.

Two flags say when a bound chose instead of the criterion:

```{r flags}
c(at_floor = sel$at_floor, at_ceiling = sel$at_ceiling)
```

```{r flag-text, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
if (isTRUE(sel$at_floor)) {
  cat("`at_floor` is `TRUE` here. Reliability wanted to keep going coarser and",
      "the correlation-range floor stopped it, so read the answer as *at most",
      "this fine* and take the number as a bound on the analysis, not as an",
      "optimum. The floor is a fact about the data, so the fix is a different",
      "question, not a different `tol`.\n")
} else {
  cat("Both are `FALSE` here, so the optimum sits inside the ladder and the",
      "criterion is the thing that chose it.\n")
}
```

Criteria can prefer different levels while agreeing on a region. `summary()`
on the profile reads the count criteria at once, and closes with the levels
that every band contains:

```{r compare-criteria}
summary(prof)
```

```{r band-text, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
# A band is a set: the curves are not monotone, so a band can skip rungs. The
# sentence below reads the rendered summary rather than quoting numbers that
# a different platform's k-means or variogram fit could move.
s     <- summary(prof)
lad   <- attr(s, "ladder")
bands <- attr(s, "bands")[s$criterion]
pos   <- lapply(bands, function(b) sort(match(b, lad)))
holed <- names(pos)[vapply(pos, function(p) any(diff(p) > 1L), logical(1))]
solid <- names(pos)[vapply(pos, function(p) length(p) > 1L && all(diff(p) == 1L),
                           logical(1))]
oxford <- function(x) if (length(x) < 2L) as.character(x) else
  paste(paste(x[-length(x)], collapse = ", "), "and", x[length(x)])
example <- if (length(holed)) {
  p <- pos[[holed[1L]]]
  skipped <- lad[setdiff(seq(min(p), max(p)), p)]
  sprintf("the `%s` band above accepts %s and rejects the %s between them,",
          holed[1L], oxford(lad[p]), oxford(skipped))
} else {
  "a band that skips a rung prints as a comma-separated list,"
}
run <- if (length(solid)) {
  p <- pos[[solid[1L]]]
  sprintf("while a solid run of %d rungs prints as a range, as `%s` does with `%d to %d`.",
          length(p), solid[1L], lad[min(p)], lad[max(p)])
} else "while a solid run prints as a range."
cat("A band is a set of levels, not an interval, because the criterion curves",
    "are not monotone:", example, run,
    "Where the bands overlap you have a defensible set of levels, and the last",
    "line names it; `attr(summary(prof), \"common\")` returns the same levels",
    "for use in code, and `attr(summary(prof), \"bands\")` each criterion's",
    "region in full. Where they do not overlap, the criteria are answering",
    "different questions and you have to say which one your analysis needs.",
    "An empty intersection is a result: it says this field has no single",
    "resolution that satisfies every way of asking.\n")
```

The table is not a decision procedure, and nothing in the package will pick
for you. Cross-validating a model at each suggested level is affordable, but
it does not settle the question either: on a simulated field the level that
won on cross-validated \(R^2\) moved with the fold seed, and the coarsest
grid won most often because its score had the widest spread, not because it
was better.

## What the ladder can support

The ladder runs from 2 cells to a ceiling the data impose. The profile records
that ceiling and, beside it, a floor from the autocorrelation range.

```{r bounds}
str(attr(prof, "bounds"))
```

The ceiling is `floor(n / min_cell_n)`, with `n` the rows that carry a
response when one is given, or the number of distinct locations
when that is smaller (one short of it when no location repeats); `ceiling_from`
says which. Past it the average cell holds too few points to estimate anything
from, or k-means has more centres to place than distinct points. The floor is `ceiling(area / range^2)`, from
the fitted autocorrelation range: cells wider than the range average over more
than one patch of the field, mixing values the field itself keeps apart. The
range is an estimate, so by default the floor is reported and not applied: it
is a level of the ladder, `select_resolution(criterion = "reliability")` reads
from it up, and `range_floor = TRUE` starts the ladder there.

When the floor exceeds the ceiling, the data cannot support a tessellation that
respects their own correlation structure. `supported` is `FALSE`, a warning says
so, and the ladder still runs from 2 to the ceiling so the cost of each level
stays visible. The usual causes are too few points for the extent, or a
correlation range shorter than the spacing between observations.

## Setting a size

The criteria above score the plain mean of a cell. `summarize_by_cell()` can
also report a *pooled* value: the cell's mean pulled toward the mean of the 8
cells around it, by a weight that grows with the number of observations the
cell holds (`estimate = "pooled"`; `vignette("reporting")` shows how to read
and report one). For that value no criterion sets the count. A *size* does:
the number of observations a cell is to hold on average, `obs_per_cell`. A
size `s` on `n` observations is `max(2, round(n / s))` cells.

`obs_per_cell` puts the profile's ladder in those terms, one level per size,
with the centres fitted to every row. `estimate` names the cell value the
profile scores:

```{r size-profile}
prof_size <- resolution_profile(pts, response_var = "z", estimate = "pooled",
                                obs_per_cell = c(12, 9, 6, 4.5, 3),
                                sac = "auto")
as.data.frame(prof_size)[, c("levels", "scored_per_cell", "loo",
                             "share_alone", "own_weight")]
```

Three of the columns say what a size leaves a cell value to stand on.

- `loo` is the leave-one-out error of the pooled value: each observation is
  predicted by the value of its cell computed without it, and the squared
  errors are averaged. It needs no variogram. `sac = "auto"` fits none on a
  ladder of sizes, so `cp` and `reliability` are `NA` in this profile.
- `share_alone` is the share of the observations that are the only one in
  their cell.
- `own_weight` is the median weight a pooled value gives its cell's own mean.
  At 1 the pooled values are the plain means; at 0 each is the mean of the
  cell's neighbours.

`select_resolution(criterion = "size")` returns the level of a size. It
searches for no optimum, so the result has no flat region and sits on no
bound:

```{r size-select}
sel_size <- select_resolution(prof_size, criterion = "size",
                              obs_per_cell = 4.5)
sel_size
```

`loo` is in the table to compare sizes by, not to choose one. For pooled
values it tends to keep falling as the cells shrink, so its minimum tends to
be the finest size offered, and the end of the ladder would then be choosing.
On 200 simulated layers of 1,500 clustered observations of a field plus noise,
profiled at seven sizes from 18 to 2, the lowest `loo` of the pooled value was
at the size 2 on 176 (`dev/sim-pooled-values.R` in the package's repository;
`?resolution_profile` gives the settings).

```{r size-text, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
lowest <- prof_size$levels[which.min(prof_size$loo)]
cat(sprintf(paste("In the table above the lowest `loo` is at %d cells, %s.\n"),
            lowest,
            if (lowest == max(prof_size$levels)) "the finest size offered"
            else "which is not the finest size offered: a tendency, not a rule"))
```

The size is therefore the caller's choice, made on other grounds: how many
observations a cell value should stand on, which `share_alone` and
`own_weight` describe. Under a size neither the cells, which are fitted to the
coordinates, nor their number, which is a count of rows, depend on the
response, so the count is not fitted to the values it will summarise.

A size does not ask whether the response has spatial structure the cells can
use, so the selection asks it separately. `structured` is `FALSE` when one
mean for the whole layer predicts a left-out observation as well as the cells
do. The count stands either way, since the caller set it, and the functions
that take the selection as a count then warn (class
`spatialkit_no_structure`) that the cell values will say little that one mean
does not.

```{r size-structured}
data.frame(structured = sel_size$structured, loo = sel_size$loo,
           one_mean = sel_size$loo_one_cell)
```

The selection goes to `get_voronoi_seeds()`, as in "Next" below. It carries a
record of how the count was set, `sel_size$count_rule`, which the seeds, the
cells and the assigned layer hand on to `summarize_by_cell()`. The summary
then checks that it reports the cell value the count was chosen for, on the
cells and rows that were scored.

## Leave-one-out for plain means

With plain means the leave-one-out error does choose a count. Each observation
is predicted by the mean of the other observations of its cell, or, when it is
alone in its cell, by the mean of the cell of its nearest other observation.
`estimate = "mean"` adds that error to the profile, and `obs_per_cell =
"auto"` then offers the seven sizes 18, 12, 9, 6, 4.5, 3 and 2:

```{r loo-profile}
prof_loo <- resolution_profile(pts, response_var = "z", estimate = "mean",
                               obs_per_cell = "auto", sac = "auto")
as.data.frame(prof_loo)[, c("levels", "scored_per_cell", "loo", "loo_se",
                            "share_alone")]

sel_loo <- select_resolution(prof_loo, criterion = "loo")
sel_loo
```

```{r loo-text, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
if (is.na(sel_loo$edge)) {
  cat(sprintf(paste("The lowest error is at %d cells, inside the sizes offered,",
                    "so the criterion chose it.\n"), sel_loo$best))
} else {
  cat(sprintf(paste("The lowest error is at %d cells, which is %s: an end of",
                    "the ladder chose the count, and the functions that take",
                    "the selection warn of it (class",
                    "`spatialkit_bound_chosen`).\n"), sel_loo$best, sel_loo$edge))
}
```

`sel_loo$flat` is every level whose error is within `tol` of the lowest, and
it is the answer to quote, as for any criterion. `loo_se` is the standard
error of one level's mean squared error. It is not the standard error of the
difference between two levels: their errors come from the same observations.

Three things to know before relying on this criterion. The count now depends
on the values of the response, so the next section applies, and
`select_on = "split"` reads `loo` on one half of the layer. The error
describes locations among the observations: it compares counts where data are
near, and says nothing about the error of a map away from them. And it sets
the count of plain means only; for pooled values a size does, as above. In
the simulation of that section the lowest `loo` of the plain mean was at the
finest size on none of the 200 layers: it was at 6 observations per cell on
86 of them, at 4.5 on 51 and at 9 on 49.

`criterion = "auto"` is the rule that goes with the profile's estimate:
`"size"` for pooled values and `"loo"` for plain means. A profile built with
`estimate` and passed straight to `get_voronoi_seeds()` as `n` is read that
way. `select_resolution()` itself still defaults to `"cp"`, which neither
profile of these two sections has, so name the criterion.

## Choosing on one half, estimating on the other

Picking the level from the same response you then aggregate is a form of
double-dipping: the cell count was chosen to suit one realisation of the field.
`select_on = "split"` profiles part of the layer and hands back the row positions
of both parts.

```{r split}
prof_split <- resolution_profile(pts, response_var = "z", n_levels = 16,
                                 select_on = "split")
sp <- attr(prof_split, "split")
sp
```

The split is spatially blocked, not random, and records the method and seed that
produced it. A random half would put neighbours of every selection point in the
estimation set, and on an autocorrelated field that leaks the structure you are
choosing against. Blocking reduces that leak without removing it: the two halves
share a border, and points on either side of it within the correlation range
are still correlated, so read the separation as a large improvement on a random
half rather than as independence.

Choose from `prof_split`, then aggregate the rows in `sp$estimation`. The cells
on the ladder are still drawn on every point, so the count it picks is a count
for the whole layer, and the ladder is as long as the full profile's. Only the
steps that read the response (the variogram, `cp`, `moran_z`) use the
selection half. The cost is power: those criteria see half the data, so the
profile is noisier and the band wider. The estimation rows also fill only
their own half of the layer: a cell inside the selection half gets none of
them, and a cell across the border between the halves is estimated from the
part of it on the estimation side. Read standard errors only off cells whose
points are all estimation rows.

```{r split-ladder}
unlist(attr(prof_split, "bounds")[c("floor", "ceiling", "n", "supported")])
```

The floor can differ from the full profile's, because it comes from the range
estimated on the selection half.

## Next

Hand the selection to whichever call decides the cell count. For a Voronoi
tessellation that is `get_voronoi_seeds()`. Given the `select_resolution()`
result itself, it returns the centres of the partition the profile scored, and a
k-means partition is the Voronoi partition of its centres, so the cells built on
those seeds are the cells the criteria judged; the bare count `sel$best` would
run a new k-means, whose cells are not. This selection sits on the range floor,
so the call warns that a bound chose the count (class
`spatialkit_bound_chosen`; warnings are not shown in this article).
`build_tessellation()` then works on the seeds:

```{r next-step}
bnd   <- clip_target_for(pts, expand = 0.02, quiet = TRUE)
seeds <- get_voronoi_seeds(boundary = bnd, method = "kmeans", n = sel,
                           sample_points = pts)
cells <- build_tessellation(seeds, boundary = bnd, method = "voronoi",
                            quiet = TRUE)
nrow(cells$cells)
```

For a lattice the count goes to `build_tessellation()` itself, and the points go
in directly:

```{r next-step-grid}
hex <- build_tessellation(pts, boundary = bnd, method = "hex",
                          approx_n_cells = sel$best, quiet = TRUE)
nrow(hex$cells)
```

The hex count overshoots the request: the target is adjusted for packing density
and then clipped to an irregular boundary, so `approx_n_cells` is approximate in
both directions. The seeded Voronoi hits the number exactly, because the seeds
are the cells.

Passing `approx_n_cells` with `method = "voronoi"` warns and is ignored. Without
the seeding step you get one cell per observation, which is a nearest-neighbour
interpolation rather than a resolution.

`vignette("spatialkit_nc_demo")` runs the whole pipeline on real boundaries.
`?resolution_profile` documents how each criterion behaved on simulated fields,
with the references; `?determine_optimal_levels` covers the k-means++ restart
budget and the nine-cell floor below which the model-aware criteria carry no
information.
